title: Battle of Carchemish
description: Nebuchadnezzar’s Babylonian forces defeated the Egyptian garrison at Carchemish. Assyria had already lost its capital, Nineveh, in 612 BC; this battle helped secure Babylonian power west of the Euphrates.
mapEffect: This helped shift control of Syria and Palestine toward Babylonia. The available territory layer has no 7th- or 6th-century BC snapshot, so the battle is shown as historical context rather than a fabricated border.

title: Babylonian conquest of Jerusalem
description: Babylonian forces captured Jerusalem, ended the kingdom of Judah’s monarchy, and destroyed the First Temple. Scholarship places the final conquest in 587 or 586 BC. The marker identifies the city, not a particular location within it.
mapEffect: Judah lost its independence, but this collection has no contemporary Judean or Babylonian border polygon. The event marker and this note communicate the change without implying a precise local boundary.

title: Cyrus captures Babylon
description: Cyrus II’s campaign defeated Babylonian forces at Opis, took Sippar, and entered Babylon. Babylon and much of its former territory passed under Achaemenid Persian rule.
mapEffect: The 500 BC Achaemenid polygon is a broad source snapshot, not a surveyed 539 BC frontier. The change of imperial control is documented; the exact border shown is approximate.

title: Battle of Gaugamela
description: Alexander defeated Darius III’s Achaemenid army on 1 October 331 BC. The exact battlefield cannot be recovered; this marker indicates the broader region east of Mosul, not a verified battle point.
confidence: battle date well-attested; battlefield location disputed
mapEffect: The battle broke Achaemenid military power, but Ptolemaic and Seleucid territories emerged through later campaigns and succession wars. The 300 BC polygons are successor-state snapshots, not borders created in one battle.

title: Pompey besieges Jerusalem
description: Pompey’s siege brought Jerusalem and Judea under Roman supremacy during Rome’s eastern campaigns. The date marks a major political transition; it does not mean Judea instantly became a standard Roman province.
mapEffect: The Roman Republic snapshot at 100 BC predates Pompey’s siege. The later Roman Empire snapshot at AD 100 does not reconstruct Judea’s local status in 63 BC, so no exact local border is drawn here.

title: Jesus in Jerusalem
description: The Gospels describe Jesus teaching and visiting the Temple in Jerusalem. This broad date range and city marker do not pinpoint a single visit or location.
